source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. XII (Montreuil)

1.title: Expositio primi capituli: In principio erat Verbum.
1.title_en: Exposition of the first chapter: “In the beginning was the Word.”

paras.t: Hoc inter theologicum philosophicumque processum, seu inter theologiam et philosophiam, distat ac interest, quod theologia seu sacra Scriptura increatæ veritati innititur, atque per lumen gratiæ revelatur; philosophia vero humanæ rationi seu naturali lumini inniti censetur, atque humano ex consideratione rerum creatarum studio invenitur. Ex quo duæ aliæ differentiæ oriuntur: Prima, quod theologiæ falsitas admisceri non valet, quoniam infallibili fundamento incumbit, et ab incommutabili Veritate infunditur ac docetur: idcirco in his quæ fidei sunt, diversa opinari vel dubitare, prorsus illicitum est. Philosophiæ vero diversi miscentur errores, propter humanæ rationis caliginem. Secunda, quod theologia exordium sumit a summo, ab ente primo, a Deo altissimo. Philosophia autem ab infimis inchoat, et paulatim ad summa conscendit: quoniam naturaliter intellectiva cognitio ex sensitiva procedit, et immaterialia atque divina per corporalia cognoscuntur, Creator quoque per creaturas, quemadmodum ad Romanos fatetur Apostolus: Invisibilia Dei per ea quæ facta sunt cognoscuntur, sempiterna quoque virtus ejus et divinitas.
paras.en: Between the theological and the philosophical way of proceeding, that is, between theology and philosophy, there is this distinction and difference: theology, or Sacred Scripture, rests on uncreated truth and is revealed through the light of grace, whereas philosophy is held to rest on human reason, or the natural light, and is discovered by human study through the consideration of created things. From this two further differences arise. The first is that no falsehood can be mingled with theology, since it rests on an infallible foundation and is infused and taught by the unchangeable Truth; therefore in matters of faith it is altogether unlawful to hold differing opinions or to doubt. With philosophy, on the other hand, various errors are mingled, because of the darkness of human reason. The second is that theology takes its beginning from the highest, from the first being, from God most high; philosophy, however, begins from the lowest things and climbs little by little to the highest, since intellectual knowledge naturally proceeds from the knowledge of the senses, and things immaterial and divine are known through bodily things, the Creator also through creatures, as the Apostle declares to the Romans: [[Rom 1:20|the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made. His eternal power also and divinity|Invisibilia Dei per ea quæ facta sunt cognoscuntur, sempiterna quoque virtus ejus et divinitas]].

paras.t: Hinc ergo excellentissimus Evangelista, qui non cognovit litteraturam, tanquam piscator et idiota, usque ad annum circiter triginta primum, de divinis, non lumine naturali, nec prævia notitia sensitiva, vel ex sensibilium consideratione instructus, sed radiante Spiritu Sancto supernaturaliter et eminentissime doctus, ab ipso universorum sublimi principio Deo sancto ac adorando, exorsus est: In principio, inquiens, erat Verbum. Nempe, quum ejus intentio fuerit, Ebionis atque Cerinthi hæreticorum, dicentium Christum esse hominem purum, hæresim reprobare, convenienter incepit a Christi divinitate, ostendens quod Christus non sit pura creatura, neque in tempore factus omnino, puta secundum se totum, sed verus Deus et Creator æternus. Itaque, In principio, id est in exordio temporis quo facta sunt omnia, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Qui vivit in æternum, creavit omnia simul. De quo principio accipi potest id Genesis: In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram. Erat Verbum, id est unigenitus Filius Dei. Quasi dicat: Inter alia non est creatum, sed illis per creationem incipientibus, ipsum veraciter erat, et invariabiliter subsistebat. Sic exponendo, excluditur error dicentium quod Christus non fuit prior Virgine Matre. Hunc quoque reor fuisse intellectum Evangelistæ, qui primo evangelii sui verbo intendebat Cerinthi et Ebionis, hæresiarcharum sui temporis, errorem destruere, asserentium Christum ex Maria sumpsisse totius sui esse initium.
paras.en: Hence the most excellent Evangelist, who knew not letters, being a fisherman and an unlettered man[[Acts 4:13||]] until about his thirty-first year, was instructed concerning divine things not by the natural light, nor by a prior knowledge through the senses, nor by the consideration of sensible things, but was taught supernaturally and most eminently by the radiance of the Holy Spirit; and so he began from the very sublime principle of all things, God, holy and adorable: [[1:1|In the beginning|In principio]], he says, [[1:1|was the Word|erat Verbum]]. For since his intention was to condemn the heresy of the heretics Ebion and Cerinthus, who said that Christ was a mere man, he fittingly began with Christ's divinity, showing that Christ is not a mere creature, nor made in time at all, that is, as regards His whole self [as man He was indeed made in time, but not as God], but true God and eternal Creator. So then: [[1:1|In the beginning|In principio]], that is, at the outset of time, when all things were made; according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 18:1|He that liveth for ever created all things together|Qui vivit in æternum, creavit omnia simul]]. Of this beginning may be taken that of Genesis: [[Gen 1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]]. [[1:1|Was the Word|erat Verbum]], that is, the only-begotten Son of God. As if to say: It was not created among the other things, but while they began through creation, It truly was, and subsisted unchangeably. Expounded thus, the error is excluded of those who say that Christ did not exist before the Virgin His Mother. This too I believe to have been the Evangelist's meaning, who in the first word of his Gospel intended to destroy the error of Cerinthus and Ebion, heresiarchs of his time, who asserted that Christ took from Mary the beginning of His whole being.

paras.t: Vel sic: In principio, hoc est ante omnia sæcula et ante tempora universa, in ipso æternitatis nunc atque momento. De quo principio scriptum est, dicente ipso Filio Dei de Patre æterno: Dominus possedit me initio viarum suarum, antequam quidquam faceret a principio. Erat Verbum, de quo Ecclesiasticus dicit: Fons sapientiæ verbum Dei in excelsis. De quo ait Apostolus: Ipse est ante omnes, et omnia in ipso constant. De hoc Verbo potest intelligi illud Isaiæ: Egredietur de ore meo justitiæ verbum. De quo per Psalmistam loquitur Deus: Eructavit cor meum verbum bonum; itemque, Verbo Domini cœli firmati sunt. Sic exponendo, confunditur error filiorum perditionis, elatissimi Arii atque Eunomii, affirmantium quod licet Filius Dei sit pura creatura, nihilo minus ante mundi creationem est genitus; et licet Patri non fuerit coæternus, tamen natura, dignitate et tempore, prior est omnibus ceteris creaturis. Horum igitur hæreticorum perfidiam sciens Joannes futuram, sic exorsus est: In principio erat Verbum.
paras.en: Or thus: [[1:1|In the beginning|In principio]], that is, before all ages and before all times, in the very now and instant of eternity [the 'now' of eternity is the schoolmen's term for eternity as a single unchanging present, without before or after]. Of this beginning it is written, the Son of God Himself speaking of the eternal Father: [[Prov 8:22|The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways, before he made any thing from the beginning|Dominus possedit me initio viarum suarum, antequam quidquam faceret a principio]]. [[1:1|Was the Word|erat Verbum]], of whom Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 1:5|The word of God on high is the fountain of wisdom|Fons sapientiæ verbum Dei in excelsis]]. Of whom the Apostle says: [[Col 1:17|he is before all: and by him all things consist|Ipse est ante omnes, et omnia in ipso constant]]. Of this Word may be understood that of Isaias: [[Is 45:23|the word of justice shall go out of my mouth|Egredietur de ore meo justitiæ verbum]]. Of whom God speaks through the Psalmist: [[Ps 44:2|My heart hath uttered a good word|Eructavit cor meum verbum bonum]]; and again: [[Ps 32:6|By the word of the Lord the heavens were established|Verbo Domini cœli firmati sunt]]. Expounded thus, the error of the sons of perdition is confounded, the most proud Arius and Eunomius, who affirmed that although the Son of God is a mere creature, He was nevertheless begotten before the creation of the world; and although He was not coeternal with the Father, yet in nature, dignity and time He is prior to all other creatures. John, therefore, knowing that the faithlessness of these heretics was to come, began thus: [[1:1|In the beginning was the Word|In principio erat Verbum]].

paras.t: Tertio sic: In principio, id est in Deo Patre, cui ratio principii appropriatur sicut æternitas, juxta illud Hilarii: Æternitas est in Patre, species in imagine, usus in munere. Pater quippe est principium sine principio, Filius vero et Spiritus Sanctus sunt principium, sed de principio. Ait enim Filius: Ego sum Alpha et Omega, principium et finis. Sciscitantibus quoque Judæis, Tu quis es? respondit: Principium, qui et loquor vobis. Denique Pater, Filius et Spiritus Sanctus, propter identitatem essentiæ sunt unum principium, una causa, unus Creator, una omnium beatitudo ac finis. Quæ enim absolute dicuntur de Deo, tribus Personis communia sunt, nec multiplicantur in eis: unde trium Personarum est unus numero intellectus, una voluntas, una potentia, justitia, misericordia atque perfectio. Itaque, In principio, Deo Patre, erat Verbum, quoniam sic procedit a Patre per generationem et personalem distinctionem, ut tamen in ipso æternaliter perseveret per substantialem identitatem. Et ut Damascenus testatur, quælibet divinarum Personarum est in alia per circumincessionem, eo quod unaquæque earum sit infinita.
paras.en: Thirdly thus: [[1:1|In the beginning|In principio]], that is, in God the Father, to whom the character of principle is appropriated, as eternity is [Latin *principium* means both 'beginning' and 'principle' or 'source'; to appropriate is to attribute especially to one Person what is in fact common to all three]; according to that saying of Hilary: Eternity is in the Father, form in the Image, use in the Gift [Hilary, *On the Trinity* II, 1: the Image is the Son, the Gift the Holy Spirit]. For the Father is a principle without a principle, while the Son and the Holy Spirit are a principle, but from a principle. For the Son says: [[Apoc 1:8|I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end|Ego sum Alpha et Omega, principium et finis]][[Apoc 21:6||]][[Apoc 22:13||]]. And when the Jews asked, [[John 8:25|Who art thou|Tu quis es]]? He answered: [[John 8:25|The beginning, who also speak unto you|Principium, qui et loquor vobis]]. Finally, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, because of the identity of their essence, are one principle, one cause, one Creator, one beatitude and end of all things. For what is said of God absolutely [that is, of the divine nature itself, not of the relations by which the Persons are distinguished] is common to the three Persons and is not multiplied in them: hence the three Persons have one intellect, numerically one, one will, one power, justice, mercy and perfection. Therefore, [[1:1|In the beginning|In principio]], in God the Father, [[1:1|was the Word|erat Verbum]], since He so proceeds from the Father by generation and personal distinction that He nevertheless remains in Him eternally by identity of substance. And as Damascene testifies, each of the divine Persons is in the other by circumincession [Greek *perichoresis*: the mutual indwelling of the three Persons in one another], because each of them is infinite.

paras.t: Rursus, emanatio in divinis, qua una Persona procedit ab alia, est emanatio ad intra, quæ non terminatur in aliud ad extra, vel substantialiter distinctum a suo fonte. Ideo Filius Dei invariabiliter manet in Patre, præsertim quum sit verbum mentale, intellectualiter profluens a corde paterno, quemadmodum scriptum est: Eructavit cor meum verbum bonum.
paras.en: Again, emanation in God, by which one Person proceeds from another, is an emanation *ad intra* [inward, within the Godhead itself, as opposed to the works *ad extra*, such as creation], which does not terminate in something outside, or substantially distinct from its source. Therefore the Son of God remains unchangeably in the Father, especially since He is a mental word [that is, a word conceived in the mind, not spoken aloud], flowing forth intellectually from the Father's heart, as it is written: [[Ps 44:2|My heart hath uttered a good word|Eructavit cor meum verbum bonum]].

paras.t: Sed nunc de ipso Verbo Dei et æterna generatione ejus, aliquid est loquendum. Et primo inquiritur, cur Evangelista volens Christi divinitatem ostendere, potius utitur nomine verbi quam filii. Hujus duplex est ratio: Prima, ut insinuet generationem in divinis non esse materialem, carnalem, seu mutationi admixtam, sed intellectualem, invariabilem, immanentem ac simplicem: quoniam verbum proprie sumptum, est interior mentis conceptus, intelligibilis dictio, atque prolata intus notitia. Alia ratio est, quoniam nomen verbi magis pertinet ad propositum quam nomen filii. Filius namque dicit comparationem dumtaxat ad patrem; verbum autem importat respectum, non tantum ad proferentem, sed etiam ad id quod per verbum exprimitur, ad vocem quoque quam induit, et ad instructionem quæ per ipsum in alio fit. Quum igitur Evangelista nunc tractet de Filio, non dumtaxat in ordine ad Patrem, sed insuper per comparationem ad creata quæ fecit et regit, præsertimque ad homines quos redemit, ad carnem quoque quam assumpsit, et ad documenta quæ dedit: constat quod convenientissime nomine verbi omnia hæc respicientis, describitur, nec aptius neque subtilius nomen ad universa hæc insinuanda invenitur.
paras.en: But now something must be said of the Word of God Himself and of His eternal generation. And first it is asked why the Evangelist, wishing to show Christ's divinity, uses the name Word rather than Son. Of this there is a twofold reason. The first is to intimate that generation in God is not material, carnal, or mixed with change, but intellectual, unchangeable, immanent and simple: since a word, taken properly, is the inward conception of the mind, an intelligible utterance, a knowledge brought forth within. The other reason is that the name Word is more to the purpose than the name Son. For son expresses a relation to the father only; but word implies a relation not only to the one who utters it, but also to what is expressed by the word, to the voice too which it puts on, and to the instruction which is brought about through it in another. Since, then, the Evangelist is here treating of the Son not only in relation to the Father, but also in relation to the created things which He made and governs, and especially to the men whom He redeemed, to the flesh too which He assumed, and to the teachings which He gave, it is plain that He is most fittingly described by the name Word, which looks to all these things, and that no apter or subtler name is to be found to intimate them all.

paras.t: Oportet autem advertere, quod verbum, secundum Damascenum, tribus modis accipitur: Primo, pro verbo vocali. Sicque dicit Gregorius, quod nihil est instabilius verbo: est enim de genere successivorum, quibus idem est esse et fieri, quemadmodum motus et tempus. Sic quoque ait Basilius: Habet autem et verbum nostrum externum divini Verbi similitudinem quamdam. Nam verbum nostrum totam declarat mentis conceptionem. Quæ namque mente concipimus, ea ore proferimus, et mens nostra quasi fons quidam est, verbum vero prolatum, quasi rivulus manans ex ipso. Secundo, pro verbo mentali quod verbo vocali exprimitur et significatur, secundum quod ait Philosophus: Sunt ergo ea quæ sunt in voce earum quæ sunt in anima passionum notæ. Unde et Plato asserit in Timæo: Ad hoc datus est nobis sermo, ut mutui atque interioris conceptus fiant indicia. Tertio, pro imaginatione vocis. Antequam enim mentale verbum verbo vocali exprimitur, formatur in sensu interiori seu virtute imaginativa, imaginatio quædam verbi vocalis, ex qua illud procedit. Imo et antequam ex auditu verbi vocalis ejus qui loquitur, verbum mentale in intellectu audientis concipitur, generatur in potentia imaginativa illius, imaginatio verbi vocalis, ex qua verbum mentale procedit: quia secundum Boetium, sicut imaginata procedunt ex sensatis, sic intellecta ex imaginatis.
paras.en: It should be noted, however, that word, according to Damascene, is taken in three ways. First, for the spoken word. And thus Gregory says that nothing is more unstable than a word: for it belongs to the class of successive things, for which to be and to come to be are the same, like motion and time. Thus too Basil says: Our outward word also has a certain likeness to the divine Word. For our word declares the whole conception of the mind; for what we conceive in the mind we utter with the mouth; and our mind is like a kind of fountain, while the word uttered is like a little stream flowing from it. Secondly, for the mental word, which is expressed and signified by the spoken word; according to what the Philosopher says: Those things that are in the voice are signs of the passions that are in the soul [Aristotle, *On Interpretation* 1; 'passions' here are the impressions or concepts of the mind]. Hence Plato too asserts in the *Timaeus*: Speech was given us for this, that it might be a sign of our inward conceptions to one another. Thirdly, for the image of the spoken word [*imaginatio*: the picture of the sound formed in the imagination]. For before the mental word is expressed by the spoken word, there is formed in the interior sense, or imaginative power, a certain image of the spoken word, from which the latter proceeds. Indeed, even before the mental word is conceived in the intellect of the hearer from hearing the spoken word of the one who speaks, there is generated in his imaginative power an image of the spoken word, from which the mental word proceeds: for according to Boethius, as things imagined proceed from things sensed, so things understood proceed from things imagined.

paras.t: Quartum modum accipiendi verbum addit Thomas, videlicet ut verbum sumatur pro re significata vel facta per verbum: quemadmodum David dixit ad puerum Amalecitam: Quod est verbum quod factum est? Sic quoque Ezechias dixit ad Isaiam: Non fuit verbum in domo mea, quod non ostenderim eis. Hoc modo cuncta creata dicuntur verba Dei, qui interiori increato ac genito Verbo, omnia intelligendo et quasi loquendo constituit, juxta illud: Ipse dixit, et facta sunt.
paras.en: Thomas adds a fourth way of taking word, namely that word be taken for the thing signified or done by the word: as David said to the Amalecite youth: [[2 Kings 1:4|What is the matter that is come to pass|Quod est verbum quod factum est]]? [Latin *verbum*, 'word', here means 'matter' or 'thing', as the Douay-Rheims renders it.] Thus too Ezechias said to Isaias: [[Is 39:4|there was not any thing which I have not shewn them|Non fuit verbum in domo mea, quod non ostenderim eis]][[Is 39:2||]] [Denis's words join 39:2, 'there was nothing', literally 'not a word', that Ezechias did not show them, with Ezechias's own answer in 39:4; the margin gives both verses]. In this way all created things are called words of God, who established all things by His inner, uncreated and begotten Word, by understanding and as it were speaking them; according to that: [[Ps 32:9|he spoke and they were made|ipse dixit, et facta sunt]][[Ps 148:5||]].

paras.t: Porro æterna generatio Verbi accipienda est ita. Quum Deus sit ens simplicissimum, nobilissimum, simpliciterque perfectum, oportet quod sit intellectualis naturæ, imo intellectus purus, semper in actu consistens. Deus ergo cognoscit se ipsum et cetera omnia. Est ergo in se ipso, sicut intellectum seu cognitum in intelligente. Intellectum vero seu res intellecta, secundum esse quod habet in intelligente, est ratio atque intentio intelligentis, et imago vel similitudo intellecti. Ratio autem et intentio seu definitio quam intelligens habet et concipit de re intellecta, vocatur verbum intelligentis, quoniam est quidam conceptus formatus atque expressio qua intra se dicit quod de re intellecta apprehendit : et hic conceptus est imago intellecti, quoniam actio intellectus perficitur in assimilatione intelligentis ad intelligibile. Hoc ergo quod Deus Pater de se ipso concipit, et intra se profert seu loquitur, appellatur Verbum mentis paternæ, et Filius Dei Patris. Emanatio itaque Verbi istius, generatio nuncupatur, et Verbum emanans vocatur Filius intelligentis intellectualiterque dicentis, quoniam generatio proprie sumpta, est productio rei viventis a vivo, quæ terminatur ad esse ejusdem naturæ secundum rationem similitudinis adæquatæ. Similiter ad rationem filii pertinet, quod procedat ex generante vitali secundum similitudinem in identitate naturæ saltem specifica. Verbum autem mentis divinæ hoc modo producitur, et cum generante convenit, non solum in specifica, sed in numerali seu individua identitate naturæ. Propter quod generatio et filiatio propriissime atque verissime habent locum in Deo, ita quod ratio patris et filii prius ac perfectius competunt Deo quam creaturis, imo a Deo derivantur secundum quamdam imitationem ad creaturas, prout Apostolus dicit : Flecto genua mea ad Patrem Domini nostri Jesu Christi, ex quo omnis paternitas in cœlo et in terra nominatur.
paras.en: Further, the eternal generation of the Word is to be understood thus. Since God is a being most simple, most noble and perfect without qualification, He must be of an intellectual nature; indeed, He must be pure intellect, always existing in act. God therefore knows Himself and all other things. He is therefore in Himself as the thing understood or known is in the one who understands. Now the thing understood, according to the being it has in the one who understands, is the concept and intention of the one who understands [ratio and intentio: the form of the thing as it exists in the mind], and the image or likeness of the thing understood. And the concept and intention, or definition, which the one who understands has and conceives of the thing understood is called the word of the one who understands, since it is a certain formed conception and expression by which he says within himself what he grasps of the thing understood; and this conception is the image of the thing understood, since the act of the intellect is perfected in the likening of the one who understands to what is understood. That, therefore, which God the Father conceives of Himself, and utters or speaks within Himself, is called the Word of the Father's mind, and the Son of God the Father. And so the emanation of this Word is called generation, and the Word that emanates is called the Son of Him who understands and speaks intellectually; for generation, properly taken, is the production of a living thing from a living thing, ending in the being of the same nature by way of an adequate likeness. Likewise it belongs to the notion of a son that he should proceed from a living begetter by way of likeness, in an identity of nature that is at least specific [that is, of the same species, as a human son shares his father's nature]. But the Word of the divine mind is produced in this way, and agrees with the One who begets Him not only in specific but in numerical or individual identity of nature. Therefore generation and sonship have their place in God most properly and most truly, so that the notions of father and son belong to God before and more perfectly than to creatures; indeed, they are derived from God to creatures by a certain imitation, as the Apostle says: [[Eph 3:14|I bow my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ|Flecto genua mea ad Patrem Domini nostri Jesu Christi]], [[Eph 3:15|Of whom all paternity in heaven and earth is named|ex quo omnis paternitas in cœlo et in terra nominatur]].

paras.t: Præterea, activa generatio Verbi, est ipsa intellectio Patris notionaliter sumpta, quæ terminatur ad Verbi productionem, seu ad ipsum verbum intus prolatum : et quoniam Pater uno simplicissimo actu se ipsum et cuncta intelligit, ideo unico actu intellectivo seu una locutione, gignit ac profert perfectissimum verbum, in quo universa resplendent, repræsentantur et continentur, quæ a Patre noscuntur, et in ejus sapientia elucescunt, fulgent ac conspiciuntur. Illud ergo unicum et simplicissimum verbum, est perfecta, itemque naturalis imago Patris, et character substantiæ ejus, tanquam ad similitudinem ejus productum, eumque plenissime repræsentans. Est quoque exemplar, species ac ratio omnium creaturarum, quoniam omnes relucent in Verbo, atque ad ejus imitationem producta sunt.
paras.en: Moreover, the active generation of the Word is the very understanding of the Father taken notionally [that is, as the act belonging to the Father as a distinct Person, not as the understanding common to the three], which ends in the production of the Word, or in the word itself uttered within. And since the Father understands Himself and all things by one most simple act, He therefore by a single act of understanding, or one speaking, begets and utters a most perfect Word, in which all things that are known by the Father, and that shine out, gleam and are beheld in His wisdom, are resplendent, represented and contained. That one and most simple Word, then, is the perfect and also natural image of the Father, and the character of His substance [character is the Greek word of Heb 1:3, where the Vulgate has figura, "figure"], as produced to His likeness and representing Him most fully. He is also the exemplar, the form and the pattern of all creatures, since all of them shine in the Word, and were produced in imitation of Him.

paras.t: Quoniam ergo tota perfectio et natura Patris perfecte relucet in Filio, quod esse non posset, nisi Filius esset vere immensus æqualisque Patri, et per consequens verus Deus, eamdem cum Patre habens essentiam (finitum namque a perfecta repræsentatione infiniti distat in infinitum); propterea Filius appellatur emanatio claritatis omnipotentis Dei, candor lucis æternæ, et speculum sine macula majestatis paternæ, atque imago bonitatis illius, quemadmodum de Filio Dei sub nomine sapientiæ scriptum est. Unde ad Hebræos ait Apostolus : Qui quum sit splendor gloriæ et figura substantiæ ejus; alibi quoque, Qui est imago Dei invisibilis.
paras.en: Since, then, the whole perfection and nature of the Father shines perfectly in the Son, which could not be unless the Son were truly immeasurable and equal to the Father, and consequently true God, having the same essence as the Father (for the finite falls infinitely short of perfectly representing the infinite), the Son is therefore called the [[Wis 7:25|emmanation of the glory of the Almighty God|emanatio claritatis omnipotentis Dei]], [[Wis 7:26|the brightness of eternal light, and the unspotted mirror|candor lucis æternæ, et speculum sine macula]] of the Father's majesty, and [[Wis 7:26|the image of his goodness|imago bonitatis illius]], as is written of the Son of God under the name of wisdom. Hence the Apostle says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 1:3|Who being the brightness of his glory and the figure of his substance|Qui quum sit splendor gloriæ et figura substantiæ ejus]]; and elsewhere, [[Col 1:15|Who is the image of the invisible God|Qui est imago Dei invisibilis]].

paras.t: Insuper, quum Filius procedat ab intellectu Patris, idcirco pertinentia ad intellectum potissime competunt Filio. Quorum aliqua sunt ei propria, et aliqua appropriata. Propria enim Filio sunt, sapientia generata, ars genita, verbum, imago : quæ omnia accipiuntur in Deo personaliter. Dum autem dicitur Verbum seu Filius Dei esse sapientia Patris et exemplar creaturarum, non est sic intelligendum, quasi Pater non sit in se et per se sapiens, sapientia ingenita, quæ est ipsemet Pater, atque exemplar, species ac ratio universorum. Alioqui, quomodo sapientem Filium generasset? Nullus enim alteri confert quod ipse non habet.
paras.en: Further, since the Son proceeds from the intellect of the Father, the things that belong to the intellect belong above all to the Son. Of these some are proper to Him and some appropriated [that is, common to all three Persons, but ascribed to one because of a likeness to what is proper to Him]. For proper to the Son are begotten wisdom, begotten art, word and image: all of which are taken in God personally. But when the Word or Son of God is said to be the wisdom of the Father[[1 Cor 1:24||]] and the exemplar of creatures, this is not to be understood as though the Father were not wise in and of Himself, with an unbegotten wisdom which is the Father Himself, and as though He were not the exemplar, form and pattern of all things. Otherwise, how could He have begotten a wise Son? For no one confers on another what he does not himself have.

paras.t: De hac æterna, divina et inenarrabili Verbi generatione habetur in Psalmo : Dominus dixit ad me : Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Et denuo : Ex utero ante luciferum genui te. In Proverbiis quoque : Ab æterno ordinata sum, et ex antiquis antequam terra fieret. Nondum erant abyssi, et ego jam concepta eram; ante colles ego parturiebar. Quando præparabat cœlos, aderam. Itemque Ecclesiasticus : Ego ex ore Altissimi prodivi, primogenita ante omnem creaturam. Hinc etiam scriptum est : Egressus ejus a principio, a diebus æternitatis. Enimvero, quod Deus ineffabilis habeat Filium ineffabilem, et per consequens sibi æqualem, clarissime innotescit ex hoc quod in libro Proverbiorum legitur : Quis suscitavit omnes terminos terræ? quod nomen ejus, et quod nomen filii ejus, si nosti?
paras.en: Of this eternal, divine and unutterable generation of the Word we have in the Psalm: [[Ps 2:7|The Lord hath said to me: Thou art my son, this day have I begotten thee|Dominus dixit ad me : Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te]]. And again: [[Ps 109:3|from the womb before the day star I begot thee|Ex utero ante luciferum genui te]]. In Proverbs too: [[Prov 8:23|I was set up from eternity, and of old, before the earth was made|Ab æterno ordinata sum, et ex antiquis antequam terra fieret]]. [[Prov 8:24|The depths were not as yet, and I was already conceived|Nondum erant abyssi, et ego jam concepta eram]]; [[Prov 8:25|before the hills, I was brought forth|ante colles ego parturiebar]]. [[Prov 8:27|When he prepared the heavens, I was present|Quando præparabat cœlos, aderam]]. And Ecclesiasticus likewise: [[Ecclus 24:5|I came out of the mouth of the most High, the firstborn before all creatures|Ego ex ore Altissimi prodivi, primogenita ante omnem creaturam]]. Hence also it is written: [[Mich 5:2|his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity|Egressus ejus a principio, a diebus æternitatis]]. And indeed, that the ineffable God has an ineffable Son, and consequently one equal to Himself, is made most clearly known by what we read in the book of Proverbs: [[Prov 30:4|who hath raised up all the borders of the earth? what is his name, and what is the name of his son, if thou knowest?|Quis suscitavit omnes terminos terræ? quod nomen ejus, et quod nomen filii ejus, si nosti?]]

paras.t: Ostenso quando erat Verbum, ostendit Evangelista ubi erat. Et Verbum erat apud Deum, id est juxta et intra Patrem, tanquam individuum inseparabileque ab eo. Non enim distant loco, duratione, natura vel dignitate; sed ubi et quando Pater, ibi et tunc Filius ejus. Quum autem dicitur, Verbum erat apud Deum, Deus accipitur relative et personaliter, non absolute et essentialiter. Quemadmodum autem Pater quum sit immensus, est illocalis et incircumscriptibilis, universa transcendens, implens, conservans ac ambiens, ita et Verbum ejus. Unde quum Verbum dicitur esse apud Patrem, non est rudite accipiendum, quasi unus sit extra et prope alium : imo totus Pater in Filio, et econtrario, vere circumincessibiliterque consistit. Sed ad designandum personalem distinctionem inter Patrem et Verbum, ait Evangelista, Verbum erat apud Deum, quasi personaliter distinctum a Patre.
paras.en: Having shown when the Word was, the Evangelist shows where He was: [[1:1|and the Word was with God|Et Verbum erat apud Deum]], that is, beside and within the Father, as undivided and inseparable from Him. For they are not apart in place, duration, nature or dignity; but where and when the Father is, there and then is His Son. And when it is said, [[1:1|the Word was with God|Verbum erat apud Deum]], "God" is taken relatively and personally, not absolutely and essentially [that is, it stands for the Person of the Father, not for the divine essence common to the three]. Now just as the Father, being immeasurable, is in no place and cannot be circumscribed, transcending, filling, preserving and encompassing all things, so too is His Word. Hence when the Word is said to be with the Father, this is not to be taken crudely, as though one were outside the other and near him: rather the whole Father is in the Son, and conversely, truly and by circumincession [that is, by the mutual indwelling of the divine Persons in one another]. But to signify the personal distinction between the Father and the Word, the Evangelist says, [[1:1|the Word was with God|Verbum erat apud Deum]], as personally distinct from the Father.

paras.t: Noverat quippe Joannes, cui totus processus ac status militantis Ecclesiæ fuerat in Apocalypsis descriptione revelatus, futuros hæreticos qui dicerent Patris et Filii eamdem esse personam. Cujus perfidiæ princeps fuit Sabellius, asserens Patrem, Filium ac Spiritum Sanctum unam esse hypostasim, tribus nominibus designatam propter diversas operationes : ita quod Deus esset Pater ratione creationis, idemque Filius ratione incarnationis, et Spiritus Sanctus ratione sanctificationis qua rationalem creaturam sanctificat. Unde Sabelliani dixerunt Patrem incarnatum ac passum : propterea dicti sunt Patrispassiani. Non enim admiserunt veram in Deo esse trinitatem vel processionem Personæ a Persona, vel Deum dici Patrem propter relationem realem; sed eo modo quo nos asserimus superbenedictam Trinitatem esse Patrem, cui incessabiliter dicimus, Pater noster qui es in cœlis. Horum errorem destruit Evangelista, dicendo, Verbum erat apud Deum : quod verum non esset, si Pater et Verbum essent una persona, quum nihil sit proprie apud se ipsum.
paras.en: For John, to whom the whole course and state of the Church militant had been revealed in the vision described in the Apocalypse, knew that there would be heretics who would say that the Father and the Son are the same person. The chief of this perfidy was Sabellius, who asserted that the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost are one hypostasis [that is, one subsisting person], designated by three names on account of different operations: so that God would be the Father by reason of creation, the same God the Son by reason of the Incarnation, and the Holy Ghost by reason of the sanctification by which He sanctifies the rational creature. Hence the Sabellians said that the Father was incarnate and suffered; and for this they were called Patripassians [from Pater, "Father", and passus, "suffered"]. For they did not admit that there is a true trinity in God, or a procession of Person from Person, or that God is called Father on account of a real relation; but only in the way in which we say that the supremely blessed Trinity is our Father, to whom we say without ceasing, [[Matt 6:9|Our Father who art in heaven|Pater noster qui es in cœlis]]. The Evangelist destroys their error by saying, [[1:1|the Word was with God|Verbum erat apud Deum]]: which would not be true if the Father and the Word were one person, since nothing is, properly speaking, with itself.

paras.t: Ostenso quando et ubi erat Verbum, declaratur quid erat. Et Deus erat Verbum. Hic sumitur Deus substantialiter et absolute, ut sit sensus : Verbum erat Deus, id est, veram habens deitatem, atque ejusdem cum suo genitore essentiæ. Unde de Filio dicit Apostolus ad Romanos : Qui est super omnia Deus benedictus in sæcula. Et in prima Joannis Canonica legitur : Simus in vero Filio ejus Jesu Christo; hic est verus Deus et vita æterna. Sicut autem in præcedenti clausula designata est inter Patrem et Verbum personalis distinctio, sic verbo præsenti insinuatur esse inter eos substantialis identitas, sive essentiæ unitas, quum nullum creatum sit Deus, sed a divinæ naturæ perfectione in infinitum deficiat. Per hoc itaque reprobatur error Photini, Arii, et omnium asserentium Filium Dei esse puram creaturam.
paras.en: Having shown when and where the Word was, the Evangelist declares what He was: [[1:1|and the Word was God|Et Deus erat Verbum]]. Here "God" is taken substantially and absolutely, so that the sense is: the Word was God, that is, having true Godhead, and of the same essence as His Begetter. Hence the Apostle says of the Son, to the Romans: [[Rom 9:5|who is over all things, God blessed for ever|Qui est super omnia Deus benedictus in sæcula]]. And in the first canonical Epistle of John we read: [[1 John 5:20|may be in his true Son|Simus in vero Filio ejus]] Jesus Christ; [[1 John 5:20|This is the true God and life eternal|hic est verus Deus et vita æterna]]. And just as in the preceding clause a personal distinction between the Father and the Word was indicated, so the present words convey that there is between them an identity of substance, or unity of essence, since nothing created is God, but falls infinitely short of the perfection of the divine nature. By this, then, is refuted the error of Photinus, of Arius, and of all who assert that the Son of God is a mere creature.

paras.t: Quod autem Filius Dei sit verus Deus, apertissime pandit Psalmista, dum ait : Sedes tua, Deus, in sæculum sæculi. Quod autem id dicatur de Filio, patet ex verbis sequentibus : Virga directionis virga regni tui, etc. Unde et Jeremias de Christo inducit : Suscitabo David germen justum, et regnabit Rex; et hoc est nomen quod vocabunt eum, Dominus justus noster. Pro quo Hebraica veritas continet nomen Domini tetragrammaton, quod (teste Rabbi Moyse) absolutissimum est, soli vero Deo conveniens. De hoc Rege fatetur Psalmista : Audi, filia, et concupiscet Rex decorem tuum, quoniam ipse est Dominus Deus tuus, et adorabunt eum. Isaias quoque de Christo Filio Dei : Parvulus, ait, natus est nobis, et vocabitur nomen ejus, Admirabilis, Consiliarius, Deus, Fortis, Pater futuri sæculi, Princeps pacis.
paras.en: That the Son of God is true God the Psalmist shows most plainly when he says: [[Ps 44:7|Thy throne, O God, is forever and ever|Sedes tua, Deus, in sæculum sæculi]]. And that this is said of the Son is clear from the words that follow: [[Ps 44:7|the sceptre of thy kingdom is a sceptre of uprightness|Virga directionis virga regni tui]], etc. Hence Jeremias too brings in [the Lord speaking] of Christ: [[Jer 23:5|I will raise up to David a just branch: and a king shall reign|Suscitabo David germen justum, et regnabit Rex]]; [[Jer 23:6|and this is the name that they shall call him: The Lord our just one|et hoc est nomen quod vocabunt eum, Dominus justus noster]]. Here the Hebrew original [Hebraica veritas, "the Hebrew truth"] has the four-lettered name of the Lord [the Tetragrammaton, YHWH], which (on the testimony of Rabbi Moses [Moses Maimonides, in his Guide of the Perplexed]) is the most absolute of names, and befits God alone. Of this King the Psalmist declares: [[Ps 44:11|Hearken, O daughter|Audi, filia]], and [[Ps 44:12|the king shall greatly desire thy beauty; for he is the Lord thy God, and him they shall adore|concupiscet Rex decorem tuum, quoniam ipse est Dominus Deus tuus, et adorabunt eum]]. Isaias also says of Christ the Son of God: [[Is 9:6|a CHILD IS BORN to us|Parvulus, ait, natus est nobis]], [[Is 9:6|and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, God the Mighty, the Father of the world to come, the Prince of Peace|et vocabitur nomen ejus, Admirabilis, Consiliarius, Deus, Fortis, Pater futuri sæculi, Princeps pacis]].

paras.t: Hoc Verbum erat in principio, id est ab æterno, in ipso æternitatis momento, vel in mundi exordio, apud Deum Patrem, tanquam coæternum eidem, sicut si sol ab æterno fuisset, vel pes in pulvere ab æterno stetisset, splendor atque vestigium æternaliter exstitissent. In his quippe quæ naturaliter profluunt, procedens seu causatum coævum est suo principio. Filius vero procedit a Patre naturali emanatione, imo a substantia Patris immediate, sine actione intermedia quæ sit realiter ab essentia Patris distincta. His itaque verbis innuitur coæternitas Patris ac Verbi.
paras.en: [[1:2|The same was in the beginning|Hoc Verbum erat in principio]], that is, from eternity, in the very instant of eternity, or at the beginning of the world, [[1:2|with God|apud Deum]] the Father, as coeternal with Him; just as, if the sun had been from eternity, or a foot had stood in the dust from eternity, the brightness and the footprint would have existed eternally [the image of the foot and its print in the dust is St Augustine's, *City of God* X, 31]. For in things that flow forth naturally, what proceeds or is caused is coeval with its principle. And the Son proceeds from the Father by a natural emanation, nay, immediately from the substance of the Father, without any intermediate action really distinct from the Father's essence. By these words, therefore, the coeternity of the Father and the Word is intimated.

paras.t: Quam Psalmista quoque evidenter ostendit, dicendo: Et permanebit cum sole et ante lunam, in generatione et generationem: itemque: Sit nomen ejus benedictum in sæcula; ante solem permanet nomen ejus. Hæc enim de nullo accipi possunt nisi de Christo Filio Regis æterni, de quo in exordio Psalmi illius cantatur: Deus, judicium tuum regi da, et justitiam tuam filio regis. Denique idem patenter ostenditur per id quod scriptum est: Ego primus, et ego novissimus; manus quoque mea fundavit terram; non a principio in abscondito locutus sum. Porro, quod ista dicantur de Filio, patet ex eo quod subditur: Et nunc Dominus misit me et spiritus ejus.
paras.en: The Psalmist also shows this clearly, saying: [[Ps 71:5|And he shall continue with the sun and before the moon, throughout all generations|Et permanebit cum sole et ante lunam, in generatione et generationem]]; and again: [[Ps 71:17|Let his name be blessed for evermore: his name continueth before the sun|Sit nomen ejus benedictum in sæcula; ante solem permanet nomen ejus]]. For these things cannot be understood of anyone but Christ, the Son of the eternal King, of whom it is sung at the opening of that Psalm: [[Ps 71:2|Give to the king thy judgment, O God, and to the king's son thy justice|Deus, judicium tuum regi da, et justitiam tuam filio regis]]. Lastly, the same is plainly shown by what is written: [[Is 48:12|I am the first, and I am the last|Ego primus, et ego novissimus]]; [[Is 48:13|My hand also hath founded the earth|Manus quoque mea fundavit terram]]; [[Is 48:16|I have not spoken in secret from the beginning|non a principio in abscondito locutus sum]]. And that these things are said of the Son is clear from what follows: [[Is 48:16|and now the Lord God hath sent me, and his spirit|Et nunc Dominus misit me et spiritus ejus]].

paras.t: Declarato quando, ubi, quid et quomodo erat Verbum, nunc manifestatur quid operabatur. Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, id est, universæ creaturæ corporales et spirituales, cœlum, terra, mare, et quidquid cœli ambitu continetur, creata sunt immediate vel mediate ab unigenito Filio Dei, sicut a causa prima, principali et efficienti. Sciendum vero, quod quandocumque dicitur aliquid fieri per aliud, præpositio, Per, designat aliquod genus causæ in causali. Dicitur autem aliquid fieri per aliud pluribus modis: Primo, sicut per causam instrumentalem: quemadmodum domus fit per securim et terebellum. Secundo, sicut per causam principalem: ut regnum gubernatur per eum quem rex fecit sibi consortem et comparem. Tertio, sicut per causam extrinsecam: ut homo percutit per baculum. Quarto, sicut per causam intrinsecam vel conjunctam: quemadmodum Petrus vivit per animam suam, et scribit per manum.
paras.en: Having declared when, where, what and how the Word was, the Evangelist now makes known what He wrought. [[1:3|All things were made by him|Omnia per ipsum facta sunt]], that is, all creatures, bodily and spiritual, heaven, earth, the sea, and whatever is contained within the compass of heaven, were created, immediately or mediately, by the only-begotten Son of God, as by their first, principal and efficient cause. Now it is to be known that whenever something is said to be made *by* [*per*, that is, through] another, the preposition *per* designates some kind of cause in the word it governs [the *causale*, the term governed by the preposition, as in St Thomas, *Summa* I, q. 36, a. 3]. And something is said to be made through another in several ways. First, as through an instrumental cause: as a house is made with an axe and an auger. Second, as through a principal cause: as a kingdom is governed by one whom the king has made his partner and equal. Third, as through an extrinsic cause: as a man strikes with a staff. Fourth, as through an intrinsic or conjoined cause: as Peter lives by his soul, and writes with his hand.

paras.t: Rursus, quum aliquid dicitur fieri per aliud, intelligi potest dupliciter: Primo, ut insinuetur mediatio quædam seu medium causans inter primum agens et effectum. Secundo, ut solum importetur processio unius ab alio: sicque fieri per aliquid, est fieri seu produci ab illo. Juxta quem modum dicit Apostolus: Paulus apostolus Jesu Christi per voluntatem Dei, id est, a divina voluntate constitutus apostolus.
paras.en: Again, when something is said to be made through another, this can be understood in two ways. First, so as to imply a certain mediation, or a causing medium between the first agent and the effect. Second, so as to convey only the procession of one from another: and in this sense to be made through something is to be made or produced by it. It is in this way that the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 1:1|Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God|Paulus apostolus Jesu Christi per voluntatem Dei]][[Eph 1:1||]][[Col 1:1||]][[2 Tim 1:1||]], that is, made an apostle by the divine will.

paras.t: Dum ergo dicuntur omnia facta per Verbum, utroque horum modorum intelligi licet, videlicet: Per Verbum, id est a Verbo, tanquam ab omnipotente Creatore, et primo universorum fontali atque causali principio: sic namque omnia facta sunt a supergloriosissima Trinitate, et a qualibet divina Persona. Item, omnia facta sunt per Verbum, tanquam per id quod inter Patrem et creaturas est medium: non tamen quasi per causam instrumentalem, ministratoriam, a Patre separatam, sive extrinsecam ei, sed sicut per causam conjunctam, parem ac principalem et effectivam. Quod rursus intelligendum non est, quasi creaturæ non sint immediate factæ a Patre, præsertim quum Pater et Filius sint una causa, unus Creator, unumque principium; sed quia Filius procedit a Patre, habens virtutem creativam ab ipso, et secundum ordinem originis mediat inter Patrem et creaturas, et quoniam Pater nil operatur ad extra sine Filio. Quum enim natura sit operationis principium, sicut trium Personarum est una natura, ita et una indivisaque actio ad extra.
paras.en: When, therefore, all things are said to have been made through the Word, this may be understood in both of these ways. Namely: through the Word, that is, by the Word, as by the almighty Creator and the first fontal and causal principle of all things; for in this way all things were made by the most supremely glorious Trinity, and by each divine Person. Again, all things were made through the Word as through that which is the medium between the Father and creatures: yet not as through an instrumental, ministering cause, separate from the Father or extrinsic to Him, but as through a conjoined cause, equal, principal and effective. Nor again is this to be understood as though creatures were not made immediately by the Father, especially since the Father and the Son are one cause, one Creator and one principle; but because the Son proceeds from the Father, having His creative power from Him, and in the order of origin stands between the Father and creatures, and because the Father does nothing *ad extra* [that is, outside the Godhead, as in creating, as distinct from the processions within it] without the Son[[John 5:19||]]. For since nature is the principle of operation, as the three Persons have one nature, so they have one undivided action *ad extra*.

paras.t: Sed quum Pater et Filius sint unus Creator et unum principium, quomodo Pater dicitur aliquid facere seu creare per Verbum vel Filium? Et respondendum, quod Pater operatur per Verbum, sicut per causam exemplarem: non quod Pater non sit causa exemplaris, imo quælibet Persona divina est omnium rerum causa efficiens, exemplaris atque finalis; sed quod Filio appropriatur ratio causæ exemplaris, eo quod sibi conveniant vi suæ emanationis, ars, sapientia, et cetera quibus convenit exemplariter agere. Quoniam ergo Pater omnia efficit per intellectum atque intelligibilem dictionem, juxta illud: Ipse dixit et facta sunt; dictio autem intus prolata, est verbum: idcirco asseritur omnia fecisse per Verbum, quamvis et per sui ipsius propriam atque ingenitam sapientiam cuncta creaverit. Itaque, omnia fecit per Verbum, non quod Pater et Verbum sint duæ causæ distinctæ, sed secundum sensum et modum prætactos, et etiam quoniam in divinis emanatio ad intra, est causa emanationis ad extra.
paras.en: But since the Father and the Son are one Creator and one principle, how is the Father said to make or create anything through the Word or Son? The answer is that the Father works through the Word as through an exemplar cause [the pattern or idea after which a thing is made]. Not that the Father is not an exemplar cause; indeed, each divine Person is the efficient, exemplar and final cause of all things; but the character of exemplar cause is appropriated [that is, attributed especially to one Person, though it belongs to all three] to the Son, because by virtue of His emanation there belong to Him art, wisdom, and the other things by which it belongs to act after an exemplar. Since, then, the Father effects all things through His intellect and an intelligible utterance, according to that saying, [[Ps 32:9|he spoke and they were made|Ipse dixit et facta sunt]][[Ps 148:5||]], and an utterance spoken within is a word, He is therefore said to have made all things through the Word, although He also created all things through His own proper and unbegotten wisdom. So He made all things through the Word, not as though the Father and the Word were two distinct causes, but in the sense and manner already touched on, and also because in God the emanation *ad intra* [the procession of the Persons within the Godhead] is the cause of the emanation *ad extra*.

paras.t: Quum vero dicimus Deum omnia fecisse in sapientia, vel per sapientiam, intelligi potest, tam de sapientia Patris ingenita, quomodo dicitur operari per ideam seu formam archetypam, quam de Sapientia genita, qui est unicus Filius ejus. Postremo, opinor quod idcirco potissimum Scriptura dicit Deum operari per Verbum et Spiritum Sanctum, ut sciamus sanctæ Trinitatis esse individuam actionem ad extra, et per consequens eamdem essentiam, sicque certissime credatur esse unus verus simplicissimus Deus.
paras.en: And when we say that God made all things in wisdom[[Ps 103:24||]], or through wisdom, this can be understood both of the unbegotten wisdom of the Father, in the way He is said to work through an idea or archetypal form, and of the begotten Wisdom, who is His only Son. Lastly, I think that Scripture says God works through the Word and the Holy Ghost chiefly for this reason: that we may know that the action of the Holy Trinity *ad extra* is undivided, and consequently that its essence is the same, and so that it may be most surely believed that there is one true and most simple God.

paras.t: Et sine ipso factum est nihil, hoc est, nulla penitus res est citra Deum, quæ non sit producta a Verbo. Itaque, per nihil, non debet intelligi creatura corporalis, vel dæmon, quoniam quidquid entitatis et bonitatis habent, a Verbo sortita sunt. Manichæus vero per nihil intellexit corporalia, quæ dixit comparatione spiritualium nihil esse, et a principio tenebrarum producta: cujus hæretica pravitas nec theologorum sanctorum, neque summorum philosophorum consonat dictis. Potest autem per nihil, peccatum intelligi, quia peccatum, quoad suum formale, nihil est, sed defectus ab ente et ordine, secundum Dionysium: ideo non est factum per Verbum, sed a voluntate creata et defectiva. Hinc ergo de Christo loquens, dicit Apostolus: In ipso condita sunt universa in cœlis et in terra, visibilia et invisibilia, sive Throni, sive Dominationes, sive Principatus, sive Potestates; omnia per ipsum et in ipso sunt creata, et ipse est ante omnes, et omnia in ipso constant.
paras.en: [[1:3|and without him was made nothing|Et sine ipso factum est nihil]], that is, there is no thing whatever below God that is not produced by the Word. Therefore by *nothing* is not to be understood bodily creatures, or the demons, since whatever being and goodness they have, they have received from the Word. Manichæus, however, understood by *nothing* bodily things, which he said were nothing in comparison with spiritual things, and were produced by the principle of darkness: a heretical depravity that agrees with the sayings neither of the holy theologians nor of the greatest philosophers. But by *nothing* sin can be understood, because sin, as to what it formally is [that is, in what makes it sin, as distinct from the act in which it is found], is nothing, but a falling away from being and from order, according to Dionysius; therefore it was not made through the Word, but by a created and defective will. Hence, then, speaking of Christ, the Apostle says: [[Col 1:16|in him were all things created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, or dominations, or principalities, or powers. All things were created by him and in him|In ipso condita sunt universa in cœlis et in terra, visibilia et invisibilia, sive Throni, sive Dominationes, sive Principatus, sive Potestates; omnia per ipsum et in ipso sunt creata]]; [[Col 1:17|And he is before all: and by him all things consist|ipse est ante omnes, et omnia in ipso constant]].

1.title: Prosecutio elucidationis primi capituli, ab eo loco quo dicitur: Quod factum est, in ipso vita erat. — In quo agitur de ideis.
1.title_en: Continuation of the explanation of the first chapter, from the place where it says: “What was made, in him was life.” In which the divine ideas are treated.

paras.t: Quamvis Verbum Patris, per quod facta sunt omnia, sit æternum, et creaturæ ex tempore vel simul cum tempore inceperint, ita quod ab agente invariabili et æterno processit recens temporalisque actio; non tamen Verbum Dei aliquo modo mutatum est: quoniam quidquid de novo produxit, per rationem æternam seu idealem præconceptionem æternaliter præordinavit quando et quomodo ipsum produceret; atque in illo instanti mundum creavit, in quo se hoc facturum ab æterno incommutabiliter præcognovit. Ex quo constat, quod vanæ ac frivolæ sunt rationes Averrois aliorumque philosophorum, æternitatem mundi probare conantium ex invariabilitate primi agentis seu Creatoris. Produxit autem Deus mundum ex tempore: Primo, secundum Thomam in Summa contra gentiles, ad declarandum quam libere esset rerum causa, ita quod omnia operatur liberrime secundum propositum voluntatis suæ, prout fatetur Apostolus ad Ephesios. Secundo, ut ex creatione rerum daretur facilis via cognoscendi æternitatem Creatoris. Quemadmodum enim Rabbi Moyses asserit: Facillima atque clarissima via probandi Deum esse, et item quod sit æternus, patet per hoc quod omnia citra ipsum de novo producta sunt. Idcirco in commemorationem beneficii creationis et æternitatis Creatoris, jussum fuit in lege celebrari sabbatum, in quo Deus ab operibus requievit.
paras.en: Although the Word of the Father, through whom all things were made, is eternal, and creatures began in time, or together with time, so that a new and temporal action proceeded from an unchanging and eternal agent, yet the Word of God was in no way changed. For whatever He produced anew, He preordained from eternity, by an eternal reason or ideal preconception, when and how He would produce it; and He created the world in that very instant in which He had unchangeably foreknown from eternity that He would do so. From this it is clear that the arguments of Averroes and of other philosophers, who try to prove the eternity of the world from the unchangeableness of the first agent or Creator, are vain and frivolous. Now God produced the world in time: first, according to Thomas in the Summa contra Gentiles, to make plain how freely He is the cause of things, so that He works all things most freely according to the purpose of His will, as the Apostle declares to the Ephesians[[Eph 1:11||]]. Second, so that the creation of things might afford an easy way of knowing the eternity of the Creator. For, as Rabbi Moses [Moses Maimonides] asserts: The easiest and clearest way of proving that God exists, and also that He is eternal, is shown by this, that all things beneath Him were produced anew. Therefore, in commemoration of the benefit of creation and of the eternity of the Creator, the law commanded that the sabbath be kept, on which God rested from His works[[Ex 20:8||]].

paras.t: Itaque ad hæc insinuanda, ait nunc gloriosissimus Evangelista: Quod factum est, id est omne creatum, in ipso Verbo vita erat, id est, in Verbo vitaliter atque intellectualiter ab æterno fuit ac splenduit, per rationem exemplarem sive ideam quam habet in Verbo omnia cognoscente intellectualiterque producente: quemadmodum artifex facit domum, et medicus sanitatem, per speciem seu exemplar domus ac sanitatis quod habet in mente. Unde, secundum Aristotelem, septimo Primæ philosophiæ, et domus et sanitas quæ sunt in materia, sunt a domo et sanitate quæ præxsistunt in intellectu. Ex his patet error Procli Platonici, Avicennæ quoque Peripatetici, et sequentium eos, affirmantium quod creata procedunt a primo principio per modum naturalis emanationis, vel essentialis emicationis, ut splendor a luce, calor ab igne, lux a sole, et rivus a fonte.
paras.en: To suggest these things, then, the most glorious Evangelist now says: [[1:3|that was made|Quod factum est]], that is, every created thing, [[1:4|In him was life|in ipso Verbo vita erat]], in the Word, that is: it was in the Word from eternity, and shone there, in the manner of life and of intellect, through the exemplar reason or idea which it has in the Word, who knows all things and produces them by His intellect; just as a builder makes a house, and a physician health, through the form or exemplar of the house and of health that he has in his mind. Hence, according to Aristotle in the seventh book of the First Philosophy [that is, the Metaphysics], both the house and the health that are in matter come from the house and the health that pre-exist in the intellect. From this the error is plain of Proclus the Platonist, and also of Avicenna the Peripatetic, and of those who follow them, who affirm that created things proceed from the first principle by way of natural emanation, or of an essential flashing forth [that is, of necessity, by nature, and not by free will], as brightness from light, heat from fire, light from the sun, and a stream from a spring.

paras.t: Esse igitur creaturarum quod habent in Verbo, imo in Patre et Spiritu Sancto totaque superbeatissima Trinitate, seu in divina essentia, est esse increatum, exemplare, causale, ideale atque vitale, vel (ut planius loquar) idea, vita et lux. Propter quod, secundum Dionysium, omnia sunt in Deo per causam et exemplar. Nempe, ut scriptum est in Elementatione theologica Procli Platonici, et in libro de Causis, quod est in alio, est in eo secundum naturam et modum ejus in quo est, et non secundum proprium esse ac modum. Quum ergo Deus sanctus et gloriosus sit mens æterna et simplicissima, certum est quod omnia sint in eo per rationem æternam ac simplicem, quæ appellatur idea et exemplar, quia per illam Deus cognoscit et operatur creata. Palam est enim quod Deus cuncta et singula propriis rationibus et speciebus intelligat ac producat.
paras.en: The being, therefore, that creatures have in the Word, or rather in the Father and the Holy Ghost and the whole most blessed Trinity, that is, in the divine essence, is an uncreated being, exemplary, causal, ideal and living; or (to speak more plainly) it is idea, life and light. For this reason, according to Dionysius, all things are in God by way of cause and exemplar. For, as is written in the Elements of Theology of Proclus the Platonist, and in the Book of Causes, what is in another is in it according to the nature and mode of that in which it is, and not according to its own being and mode. Since, then, God, holy and glorious, is an eternal and most simple mind, it is certain that all things are in Him by an eternal and simple reason, which is called idea and exemplar, because through it God knows and makes created things. For it is plain that God understands and produces all things, each and every one, by their proper reasons and forms.

paras.t: Sed quum Deus sit simplicissima unitas, quomodo potest in eo esse exemplarium rationum multitudo, et idearum pluralitas atque distinctio? Et respondendum, quod idea est divina essentia a divino intellectu per modum imitabilis ac repræsentativi intellecta. Divina quippe essentia, quum sit perfectionis immensæ, omnium rerum perfectionem causaliter continens et supereminenter complectens, ab omnibus creaturis, secundum aliquem gradum perfectionis, participatur et imitatur; omnia quoque intellectualiter repræsentat. In quantum ergo intellectus divinus cognoscit divinam essentiam, vel Deus se ipsum ut participabilem a tali vel tali ente creato, sive creabili vel creando, secundum hoc divina essentia habet rationem ideæ, et nuncupatur idea rei creatæ, quæ per eam cognoscitur et causatur. Suntque in Deo multæ atque distinctæ ideæ, non quod in Deo sit diversitas aliqua vel distinctio idearum ex parte Dei; sed distinctio ista est ex parte rerum ideatarum, ad quas refertur idea: quæ tamen relatio realis non est, sed rationis ex parte ideæ, quamvis ex parte ideatorum consistat realis.
paras.en: But since God is the most simple unity, how can there be in Him a multitude of exemplar reasons, and a plurality and distinction of ideas? The answer is that an idea is the divine essence as understood by the divine intellect in the manner of something that can be imitated and that represents. For the divine essence, being of boundless perfection, containing causally and embracing supereminently the perfection of all things, is shared in and imitated by all creatures, each according to some degree of perfection; and it also represents all things intellectually. Inasmuch, then, as the divine intellect knows the divine essence, or God knows Himself, as able to be shared in by this or that created being, whether creatable or to be created, to that extent the divine essence has the character of an idea, and is called the idea of the created thing, which is known and caused through it. And there are in God many and distinct ideas: not that there is any diversity or distinction of ideas on the part of God, but this distinction is on the part of the things modelled on the ideas, to which the idea is referred. This relation, however, is not real but of reason on the part of the idea, though on the part of the things modelled on it it is real [a relation of reason exists only in the mind's way of considering a thing; so God is not really changed or multiplied by His relation to creatures, while creatures are really related to Him].

paras.t: De his exemplaribus rationibus ac idealibus formis, professus est Plato in primo Timæi, dicendo: Certe dubium non est ad cujusmodi exemplum animadverterit mundani operis fundamenta constituens: nam si (ut utique est) pulchritudine incomparabili mundus est, opifexque et fabricator ejus optimus, perspicuum est quod juxta sinceræ et incommutabilis proprietatis exemplum, mundi sit instituta molitio. — Hinc denique Augustinus, in libro LXXXIII Quæstionum: Ideas (inquit) Plato primus appellasse perhibetur; non tamen rem ipsam ipse primus cognovit, quoniam tanta vis constituitur in ideis, ut nisi his intellectis, sapiens esse nemo possit. Sunt namque ideæ principales formæ vel rationes rerum stabiles atque incommutabiles, quæ ipsæ formatæ non sunt, ac per hoc æternæ sunt, semper eodem modo sese habentes, quæ in divina intelligentia continentur. Et quum ipsæ neque oriantur, neque intereant, secundum eas tamen formari dicitur omne quod oriri et interire potest. Has autem rationes ubi esse arbitrandum est, nisi in mente Creatoris? Non enim extra se aliquid intuebatur, ut secundum illud constitueret quod constituebat. Ex quibus constat, quod quidam dicentes ideam esse rem creatam et cognitam objectaliter contemplatam, non rationem in luce divinæ mentis exsistentem, contradicunt Augustino.
paras.en: Of these exemplar reasons and ideal forms Plato spoke openly in the first part of the Timaeus [in the Latin version of Chalcidius], saying: Certainly there is no doubt to what kind of exemplar he looked when he laid the foundations of the work of the world: for if (as indeed it is) the world is of incomparable beauty, and its maker and builder the best, it is evident that the building of the world was set up according to an exemplar of pure and unchangeable character. And so Augustine, in the book of Eighty-three Questions [q. 46], says: Plato is held to have been the first to name the ideas; yet he was not the first to know the thing itself, since such power is set in the ideas that no one can be wise unless he has understood them. For the ideas are certain principal forms or reasons of things, stable and unchangeable, which are not themselves formed, and are therefore eternal, always remaining the same, and which are contained in the divine understanding. And though they themselves neither come to be nor pass away, yet everything that can come to be and pass away is said to be formed according to them. But where are these reasons to be thought to be, if not in the mind of the Creator? For He did not look at anything outside Himself, so as to make what He made according to it. From this it is clear that certain men who say that an idea is a created thing, known and contemplated as an object, and not a reason existing in the light of the divine mind, contradict Augustine.

paras.t: Insuper Origenes hic ait: Potest et sic distingui, Quod factum est in ipso; et postea dicatur, Vita erat: ut sit sensus: Omnia per ipsum et in ipso facta sunt, et in ipso unita sunt et unum sunt. In ipso enim erant, quia in ipso subsistunt causaliter priusquam sint in semetipsis effective. Sed si quæsieris, quomodo et qua ratione omnia quæ per Verbum facta sunt, in ipso vitaliter et uniformiter atque causaliter subsistunt, accipe exemplum ex creaturarum natura. Conspice quomodo omnium rerum quas mundi hujus sensibilis globositas comprehendit causæ, simul et uniformiter in sole, qui est maximum mundi luminare, subsistunt; quomodo numerositas herbarum et fructuum, in singulis seminibus simul continetur; quomodo multiplices regulæ, in arte artificis unum sunt; quomodo infinitus linearum numerus, in uno puncto unum subsistit. Ex his naturalibus exemplis, velut philosophiæ theoriæ pennis, poteris arcana Verbi acie mentis inspicere, et quantum datur humanis rationibus, videre quomodo omnia quæ per Verbum sunt facta, in ipso vivunt et facta sunt.
paras.en: Moreover, Origen [that is, the homily on the prologue of John that went under his name; it is by John Scotus Eriugena] says here: It can also be divided thus, [[1:3|that was made|Quod factum est]] in him; and then is said, [[1:4|was life|Vita erat]]; so that the sense is: All things were made through Him and in Him, and in Him they are united and are one. For they were in Him, because they subsist in Him causally before they are in themselves in effect. But if you ask how, and in what way, all things that were made through the Word subsist in Him living, uniformly and causally, take an example from the nature of creatures. See how the causes of all the things that the globe of this sensible world contains subsist together and uniformly in the sun, which is the greatest light of the world; how the multitude of plants and fruits is contained all together in each of their seeds; how many rules are one in the art of the craftsman; how an infinite number of lines subsists as one in a single point. From these natural examples, as on the wings of philosophical contemplation, you will be able to look into the secrets of the Word with the eye of the mind, and, so far as is granted to human reasons, to see how all things that were made through the Word live in Him and were made.

paras.t: Postremo sciendum, quod in tribus Personis et unaquaque earum, sit eadem ratio exemplaris atque indistincta idea. Itaque omne quod factum est, fit vel fiet, est vita in Verbo, id est, secundum vitalem ideam præxsistit in ipso: et hæc vita est divina essentia, quæ est vita et lux.
paras.en: Lastly, it must be known that in the three Persons, and in each of them, there is the same exemplar reason and one undivided idea [the ideas belong to the divine essence, common to all three Persons; they are said to be in the Word by appropriation, since the Word is the Father's conception]. So everything that has been made, is made or will be made, is life in the Word, that is, it pre-exists in Him according to its living idea; and this life is the divine essence, which is life and light.

paras.t: Et vita erat lux hominum. Hic sumitur vita personaliter pro hypostasi Verbi, seu ipso Verbo subsistente. Vita, id est, Verbum Dei vivens, et vitæ principium (de quo legitur : Quoniam apud te est fons vitæ), erat lux hominum, hoc est dator luminis naturalis ingenii, atque infusor luminis gratiæ. Quidquid enim intellectualis claritatis, decoris et perfectionis in hominibus reperitur, a Verbo seu Filio Dei profluxit et datur, a quo dona naturæ et gratiæ derivantur. Dicitur ergo Verbum lux nostra, quasi causa nostræ illustrationis, illuminans nos ad divinorum cognitionem, atque perducens ad beatitudinem supernaturalem per supernaturalia dona Spiritus Sancti, sicut ait Apostolus : Gratia Dei vita æterna. Hinc dicit Psalmista : Signatum est super nos lumen vultus tui, Domine.
paras.en: [[1:4|And the life was the light of men|et vita erat lux hominum]]. Here “life” is taken personally, for the hypostasis of the Word, that is, for the Word Himself as subsisting [that is, as a distinct Person, not as a quality or attribute]. The life, that is, the living Word of God and the principle of life (of whom we read: [[Ps 35:10|For with thee is the fountain of life|quoniam apud te est fons vitæ]]), was the light of men, that is, the giver of the light of natural understanding and the one who pours in the light of grace. For whatever intellectual brightness, beauty and perfection is found in men has flowed from, and is given by, the Word or Son of God, from whom the gifts of nature and of grace are derived. The Word is therefore called our light, as being the cause of our enlightenment, enlightening us to the knowledge of divine things and leading us on to supernatural beatitude through the supernatural gifts of the Holy Ghost; as the Apostle says: [[Rom 6:23|the grace of God, life everlasting|Gratia autem Dei, vita æterna]]. Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 4:7|The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us|Signatum est super nos lumen vultus tui, Domine]].

paras.t: Sed quoniam, juxta divinum Dionysium, nulla creatura sit expers participationis lucis divinæ, cur Verbum seu vita hæc appellatur specialiter lux hominum? Et respondendum dupliciter : Primo, quia in hoc libro tractatur de Verbo prout salvator est generis humani, eripiens nos a tenebris ignorantiæ et peccati, transferensque ad lumen gratiæ in præsenti, atque ad lumen gloriæ in futuro. Secundo, quoniam inter omnes creaturas corporales et inferiores, solus homo ad Deum convertitur et pertingit per intellectum et voluntatem : idcirco specialiter illustratur a Verbo, tanquam ad Dei imaginem factus.
paras.en: But since, according to the divine Dionysius, no creature is without some share in the divine light, why is the Word, or this life, called specially the light of men? The answer is twofold. First, because this book treats of the Word as He is the Saviour of the human race, snatching us from the darkness of ignorance and sin and bringing us over to the light of grace in the present[[1 Pet 2:9||]], and to the light of glory in the future. Secondly, because among all the bodily and lower creatures man alone turns to God and reaches Him by understanding and will; therefore he is specially enlightened by the Word, as being made to the image of God.

paras.t: Et lux ista, videlicet Verbum, de quo cantamus in Psalmo : In lumine tuo videbimus lumen ; in tenebris lucet, hoc est, inter perversos Judæos conversatione, prædicatione et signis resplenduit. Vel, In tenebris lucet, hoc est, in cordibus impiorum gratiæ suæ lucem diffundit, et per prædicatores fideles hominibus excæcatis ac reprobis lumen christianæ doctrinæ proponit. Potest quoque per tenebras, omnis creatura intellectualis intelligi, quæ comparatione lucis divinæ, potius reputatur caligo quam lux. Propter quod ait Psalmista : Deus meus, illumina tenebras meas.
paras.en: [[1:5|And the light|Et lux]], namely the Word, of whom we sing in the Psalm, [[Ps 35:10|in thy light we shall see light|in lumine tuo videbimus lumen]], [[1:5|shineth in darkness|in tenebris lucet]], that is, shone forth among the perverse Jews by His manner of life, His preaching and His signs. Or, [[1:5|shineth in darkness|in tenebris lucet]], that is, He pours the light of His grace into the hearts of the wicked, and through faithful preachers sets the light of Christian doctrine before blinded and reprobate men. By the darkness, too, may be understood every intellectual creature, which in comparison with the divine light is reckoned darkness rather than light. That is why the Psalmist says: [[Ps 17:29|O my God, enlighten my darkness|Deus meus, illumina tenebras meas]].

paras.t: Et tenebræ eam non comprehenderunt. Infra ait S. Joannes, quod cohors et tribunus et ministri Judæorum comprehenderunt Jesum. Et in Actibus princeps Apostolorum ait de Juda : Qui fuit dux eorum qui comprehenderunt Jesum. Nonne et isti tenebræ exstiterunt, quibus dixit Salvator, Hæc est hora vestra et potestas tenebrarum? Quomodo ergo tenebræ non comprehenderunt hanc lucem? Sed hoc facillime solvitur, quoniam illa de corporali comprehensione Christi intelliguntur, nunc autem de spirituali comprehensione fit sermo.
paras.en: [[1:5|And the darkness did not comprehend it|et tenebræ eam non comprehenderunt]]. Further on St. John says that [[John 18:12|the band and the tribune and the servants of the Jews took Jesus|cohors et tribunus et ministri Judæorum comprehenderunt Jesum]] [Denis plays on *comprehendere*, which means both “to seize, arrest” and “to grasp, understand”; it is the verb of v. 5 and of the two passages he cites, where the Douay-Rheims has “took” and “apprehended”]. And in the Acts the prince of the Apostles says of Judas: [[Acts 1:16|who was the leader of them that apprehended Jesus|qui fuit dux eorum qui comprehenderunt Jesum]]. Were not these too darkness, to whom the Saviour said, [[Luke 22:53|this is your hour and the power of darkness|hæc est hora vestra, et potestas tenebrarum]]? How then did the darkness not comprehend this light? But this is very easily solved: those passages are understood of the bodily seizing of Christ, whereas here the discourse is of spiritual comprehension.

paras.t: Verum tunc rursus quæstio oritur, quomodo tenebræ non comprehenderunt hanc lucem. Multi enim ad Christum conversi sunt, eumque per fidem, spem et caritatem comprehenderunt : quibus dicit Apostolus, Fuistis aliquando tenebræ, nunc autem lux in Domino. Sed rursus apparet oppositum. Ut enim mox subjungetur, Deum nemo vidit unquam : ergo multo amplius Deum nemo comprehendit unquam, quum spiritualis comprehensio sit perfectissima, interna ac intima visio. Et respondendum, quod Evangelista ad litteram loqui videtur de obtenebratis Judæis, et comprehensione Christi per fidem et caritatem. Sic enim excæcati et indurati Judæi Christum non comprehenderunt. Unde Salvator ad eos : Sermo (inquit) meus non capit in vobis ; et iterum, Neque me scitis, neque Patrem meum.
paras.en: But then the question arises again: how did the darkness not comprehend this light? For many were converted to Christ and comprehended Him by faith, hope and charity; to whom the Apostle says, [[Eph 5:8|you were heretofore darkness, but now light in the Lord|aliquando tenebræ, nunc autem lux in Domino]]. And yet the opposite appears again. For, as will be added shortly, [[1:18|No man hath seen God at any time|Deum nemo vidit umquam]]: much more, then, has no man ever comprehended God, since spiritual comprehension is the most perfect, inward and intimate vision. The answer is that the Evangelist seems, according to the letter, to be speaking of the darkened Jews, and of the comprehension of Christ by faith and charity. For in this way the blinded and hardened Jews did not comprehend Christ. Hence the Saviour says to them: [[John 8:37|my word hath no place in you|sermo meus non capit in vobis]]; and again, [[John 8:19|Neither me do you know, nor my Father|Neque me scitis, neque Patrem meum]].

paras.t: Præterea, multiplex est comprehensio. Prima est comprehensio terminativa, qua res secundum se totam capitur, videtur sive cognoscitur, tam perfecte sicut cognoscibilis est. Sicque infinitum a finito comprehendi non valet. Unde hoc modo Deus est tam incomprehensibilis omni creaturæ, etiam Sanctis in patria, quam immensus : ideo hoc modo ipse solus comprehendit se ipsum. Secunda est comprehensio claræ visionis, qua essentia rei vere conspicitur. Et ita Beati comprehendunt Deum, quem facie ad faciem contuentur : propter quod comprehensores dicuntur. Tertia est comprehensio certæ adhærentiæ per fidem, atque sinceræ adhæsionis per caritatem. Sic viatores comprehendunt Deum : quod magis proprie dicitur apprehendere quam comprehendere. Tenebræ ergo, id est peccatores, quia in suis malitiis permanserunt, nullo horum modorum comprehenderunt Jesum. Qui autem conversi sunt, comprehenderunt eum tertio modo.
paras.en: Moreover, comprehension is manifold. The first is terminative comprehension [that is, comprehension that reaches the limit of its object and encloses it wholly], by which a thing is grasped, seen or known according to the whole of itself, as perfectly as it is knowable. In this way the infinite cannot be comprehended by the finite. Hence in this way God is as incomprehensible to every creature, even to the Saints in the fatherland, as He is immense; and so in this way He alone comprehends Himself.
